title: Tropical IPA Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What a tropical IPA is, which hops and yeast give mango and passion fruit flavours and how to taste one in Indian heat.
teaser: Mango, passion fruit, pineapple and not a single piece of fruit in the tank. Here is how tropical IPAs do it.
standfirst: Tropical IPA is a name brewers use for IPAs that taste of mango, pineapple, guava and passion fruit. Sometimes the fruit is real. More often it comes from hops and yeast. Here is what is going on and how to taste one well.
sections: A name, not an official style

You will not find tropical IPA as a separate category in the major style guidelines. It is a descriptive label. Brewers use it for IPAs built around tropical fruit flavours, whether those come from hops, yeast, actual fruit or all three.

Most tropical IPAs fall within the broad American IPA family, either clear and bitter like a West Coast IPA or hazy and soft like a New England IPA. Typical strength is around 6 to 7.5% ABV, with bitterness anywhere from about 30 to 70 IBU depending on which side of that family the brewer leans.
The hops that taste like fruit

Modern hop breeding produced varieties with strong fruit character. Citra is known for mango, lychee and citrus. Mosaic brings tropical and berry notes. Galaxy from Australia is famous for passion fruit. Nelson Sauvin from New Zealand gives white grape and gooseberry. Brewers blend these to build a fruit bowl in the glass.

Most of that aroma comes from late additions: hops added at the end of the boil, in a whirlpool below boiling or as a dry hop in the fermenter. Dry hopping rates in hop-forward IPAs often run to several grams per litre. Bitterness comes mainly from the early boil additions, so brewers can push aroma without making the beer harsh.
Thiols and the passion fruit effect

Some of the most striking tropical aromas come from sulphur-containing compounds called thiols. In tiny amounts they smell of passion fruit, grapefruit and guava. Hops contain some free thiols and a larger store bound to other molecules where the nose cannot detect them.

Certain yeast strains can release those bound thiols during fermentation, part of what brewers call biotransformation. Newer engineered yeasts are designed to release far more. Our guide to thiolised yeast explains how they work. This is why two beers with the same hops can taste quite different.

Thiols are powerful. Some can be detected by the human nose at concentrations measured in nanograms per litre, which is why a small change in yeast or hop lot shows up so clearly in the glass. At high levels the same compounds can tip over from passion fruit into something sweaty or catty, so balance matters.
Yeast esters add their own fruit

Yeast contributes fruit independently of hops. Ale yeasts produce esters, compounds that smell of banana, pear, peach or apricot. English and some hazy IPA strains produce more esters than the clean American strains used for West Coast beers.

Fermentation temperature shapes this. A strain fermented at 20 °C behaves differently from the same strain at 18 °C. Brewers adjust temperature to dial the ester level up or down, so the yeast fruit supports the hop fruit rather than clashing with it.

Some tropical IPAs do contain fruit, usually purée added after fermentation. Mango, pineapple, passion fruit and guava are common. Fruit adds aroma, colour and some acidity, though its sugar also ferments and can raise the alcohol a little.

Indian brewers have an advantage here, with fresh Alphonso mangoes, guava and passion fruit close at hand. The risk is that fruit hides weak hopping or sloppy fermentation. A tropical IPA should still taste like an IPA, with hop bitterness and a dry finish, not like a fruit cooler.

Food helps the style shine. A tropical IPA next to a coconut-based Kerala fish curry or Goan prawn balchão works well, the fruit aroma meeting the coconut while the bitterness cuts the richness. Spicy food does push bitterness up, so a softer hazy version often suits chilli-heavy dishes better than a sharp West Coast one.

Tropical hop aromas are among the first flavours to fade. Heat and oxygen dull them quickly, turning bright mango into something closer to onion or cardboard. In Indian conditions, where cans can sit at 35 °C in a shop or truck, a tropical IPA can lose much of its character within weeks.

Buy from places that keep beer cold, check the packaging date and drink within a few weeks of canning. If a tropical IPA smells of garlic or tastes muddy and harsh, it has probably been stored warm. Serve at around 6 to 8 °C in a tulip glass.

Telling mango from passion fruit from guava in a beer is harder than it sounds. Most people reach for the word tropical and stop there. Trained tasters build a reference library by smelling real fruit next to beer and learning which aromas come from hops, yeast or added fruit. That kind of guided practice is the heart of sensory training.

For a first step, buy a mango, a passion fruit and a guava. Smell each one, then smell a fresh tropical IPA. Write down which fruit you find first and which you find only after a minute.
faqs: Hops such as Citra, Mosaic and Galaxy, yeast esters and thiols give mango, passion fruit and pineapple aromas. Some brewers also add real fruit.
Is tropical IPA an official style?
No. It is a descriptive label. Most tropical IPAs fall within the American or hazy IPA categories.
Some do, but many get their fruit flavour entirely from hops and yeast.
Why does my tropical IPA taste of onion?
Old or warm-stored hop-forward beer can develop onion or garlic notes as the bright fruit aromas fade.
